asparagus-canned-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Asparagus, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned asparagus consists of selected spears that are blanched and sealed in airtight jars without any added fat. The process retains most of the vegetable’s nutrients, its delicate flavor, and a pleasant bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and is one of the oldest known vegetables.
Canning extends its shelf life to 2–3 years while preserving quality.
In the United States, canned asparagus ranks among the top ten most consumed canned vegetables.
Canned spears are a convenient shortcut for soups, stews, and salads.
Asparagus is rich in antioxidants, especially glutathione.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides roughly 20 kcal, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Glutathione and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned vegetables often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Large amounts of asparagus can increase vitamin K levels, potentially affecting anticoagulant medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the spears cold in salads, toss them into pasta, omelets, or soups. Open the jar, drain the liquid, and if desired, quickly heat on a skillet or in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, transfer the asparagus to an airtight container and keep refrigerated, using within 3–4 days.

cereal-or-granola-bar-with-yogurt-coatin.title: Nature Valley Chewy Granola Bar with Yogurt Coating

content.title: About
content.content: The Nature Valley Chewy Granola Bar with yogurt coating from General Mills is a soft granola bar covered in a creamy yogurt glaze. It contains whole oat flakes, sunflower seeds, honey, and a thin layer of yogurt coating that gives a sweet‑tart flavor. The product is marketed as a convenient snack for active lifestyles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nature Valley was launched in 1975 and is known for both crunchy and chewy granola bars.
The yogurt coating was introduced in the early 2020s to broaden the flavor portfolio.
Each bar weighs 42 g and provides about 190 calories.
The recipe uses whole oat flakes rather than processed oats, preserving texture and nutrients.
The bar contains no artificial colors, but may have trace amounts of nuts and soy.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole oat flakes are rich in beta‑glucan, which supports heart health and helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: Probiotic yogurt coating
items.content: The yogurt glaze may contain live cultures that promote gut health.

items.title: Honey sweetener
items.content: Honey provides a quick source of energy and contains antioxidants.

items.title: Plant‑based protein
items.content: The bar delivers about 4 g of protein, aiding muscle maintenance for active people.

items.title: Contains vitamin D and calcium
items.content: The yogurt coating adds a modest amount of calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: The yogurt coating contains dairy, making the bar unsuitable for those with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: With roughly 12 g of sugar per bar, it may be a concern for individuals monitoring glucose levels.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Manufactured on lines that also process nuts and soy, so trace allergens may be present.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Regular consumption can contribute to weight gain if not accounted for in the overall daily calorie budget.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is ready to eat straight from the package as a quick snack, can be chopped into yogurt or kefir, or used as a sweet component in trail mixes and breakfast bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly to prevent moisture absorption. For extended storage (over 6 months), keep in the refrigerator.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-rotisserie-skin-ea.title: Chicken, NS as part, rotisserie, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. In this case it refers to the “NS” part prepared on a rotisserie, with the skin left on and considered edible. This method keeps the meat juicy while the skin becomes crispy and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rotisserie cooking distributes heat evenly, resulting in tender meat.
Chicken skin contains beneficial fats that can be part of a balanced diet when cooked properly.
Rotisserie chicken is a tradition in many cultures, from Mediterranean to Asian cuisines.
The “NS” chicken cut is often used in fast‑food and street‑food dishes.
When marinated and roasted correctly, the skin can be a source of vitamin E.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat in lean meat
items.content: Skin‑less chicken breast contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immune health.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: When eaten in moderation, chicken skin provides monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol in the skin
items.content: Chicken skin contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: High sodium in prepared products
items.content: Pre‑marinated rotisserie chickens often contain added salt; check labels if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rotisserie “NS” chicken can be served hot, sliced into pieces, added to salads, sandwiches, or enjoyed as a standalone snack. The skin can be eaten together with the meat for added crunch and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it remains good for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney is a culinary organ commonly used in various cuisines around the world. It has a tender, slightly sweet texture and a flavor reminiscent of meat. Kidneys are usually prepared fried, stewed, or roasted and often served sliced as rings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kidneys are a popular dish in European, Asian, and Latin American cooking.
Roasted kidneys are considered rich in iron and B‑vitamins.
In some cultures kidneys are made into pâtés or used as fillings for pies.
Kidneys can come from beef, pork, or veal, each offering a distinct taste.
Traditionally kidneys are soaked in milk or water to remove bitterness.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in kidneys supports hemoglobin formation and helps maintain energy levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Kidneys contain B12, B2 and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Kidneys provide complete animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and participates in wound healing.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat cuts, kidneys have relatively low fat content.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to kidneys.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Purines can raise uric acid levels, which is undesirable for people with gout.

items.title: Toxin risk if not properly prepared
items.content: Raw kidneys may contain toxins and must be thoroughly cooked.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Kidneys contain cholesterol, so those with cardiovascular concerns should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kidneys are usually cleaned of membranes, cut into pieces and quickly seared over high heat, stewed with vegetables, or baked in the oven. They are often soaked in milk or water before cooking to reduce bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh kidneys keep in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in an airtight bag where they retain quality for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen kidneys in the refrigerator before use.
